text:
Recent work supports claim-level grounding but does not establish a validated taxonomy covering compatibility, redundancy, and recent interest together. [QASemConsistency (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07473) localizes fine-grained factual inconsistencies and reports human annotation agreement κ>0.7. [AmbiFC (2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.1/) shows that underspecification can produce conflicting yet valid interpretations. [FIRE (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05225) distinguishes plausible recommendation explanations from explanations grounded in model decisions; its review-based approach cannot transfer directly to this task’s restricted inputs. [Abstention research (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12452) finds that permission to abstain alone does not reliably prevent unsupported answers.

A proposed adaptation for the twenty users: annotate each recommendation against timestamped training histories, recording item IDs, exact title/description spans, and separate supported/contradicted/unknown judgments. Mark specification conflict only when explicit requirements and specifications clash; historical interaction alone does not establish ownership or a compatibility requirement. Mark functional overlap descriptively, without assuming redundancy is unwanted. Record recent-interest connections through explicit shared attributes and a predefined recency window, without inferring satisfaction or intent. Missing evidence means unknown, not incompatibility or irrelevance. Have two humans independently annotate a shared sample; report raw agreement, label agreement, evidence-span overlap, and unknown rates before adjudication. This reliability check matters because [Liu et al. (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.inlg-main.48/) found annotation method affected hallucination detection and agreement. These annotations would be descriptive diagnostics, not observed simulator traits, causal failure labels, or substitutes for macro validation HR@10.
